etymology: James 3:17 — sophia anōthen — wisdom from above.
biblical_def: James's seven-fold portrait of true wisdom: pure, peaceable, gentle, easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, without hypocrisy (James 3:17); contrasted with earthly, sensual, devilish wisdom (3:15).
webster_summary: James's seven-fold portrait of true wisdom.
webster_full: The wisdom that comes down from the Father of lights, contrasted in James 3 with earthly, sensual, devilish wisdom; characterized by seven marks: first pure, then peaceable, gentle, willing to yield, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial, and without hypocrisy.
scriptures: James 3:17
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
James 3:15
This wisdom descendeth not from above, but is earthly, sensual, devilish.
James 1:17
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights.
corruption_summary: Reduced to inspirational sentiment; James gives a sharp diagnostic checklist.
corruption_paragraphs: James 3:17 is a diagnostic. Apply it: is your wisdom pure-first? peaceable? gentle? willing to yield? merciful? impartial? un-hypocritical? Wisdom from below comes with envy and strife; wisdom from above comes with the seven marks. Test your wisdom by James's list.
roots_summary: Greek sophia anōthen — wisdom from above.

etymology: Biblical figure traced through Psalm 1, Matthew 7, and the Didache.
biblical_def: The wisdom-tradition image of two paths laid before every life: the way of righteousness leading to life, and the way of wickedness leading to destruction (Ps 1; Prov 4:18-19; Matt 7:13-14).
webster_summary: The wisdom-image of two paths: life or death.
webster_full: The biblical wisdom figure of two paths laid before every life — the way of righteousness leading to life, and the way of wickedness leading to destruction; framed by Psalm 1, repeated in Proverbs, climaxed by Christ's narrow-and-broad gates in the Sermon on the Mount, and structured the early Christian Didache.
scriptures: Psalm 1:6
For the LORD knoweth the way of the righteous: but the way of the ungodly shall perish.
Matthew 7:13-14
Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction... Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life.
Deuteronomy 30:19
I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life.
corruption_summary: Replaced by 'all paths lead to God' relativism; Scripture insists there are two ways with two destinations.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern pluralism wants many paths to one mountaintop. Scripture insists on two paths with two destinations. Walk one and live; walk the other and perish. The image runs through every layer of revelation. Choose life.
roots_summary: Hebrew derek — way; Greek hodos — way.
usage: Choose life; walk the narrow way.

etymology: Greek diakriseis pneumatōn — judging-distinctions of spirits.
biblical_def: The spiritual gift listed by Paul (1 Cor 12:10) for distinguishing true from false spiritual influence; required of the church in evaluating prophecy, teaching, and spiritual claims (1 John 4:1).
webster_summary: Spirit-given ability to distinguish true from false spiritual influence.
webster_full: The Spirit-given ability to distinguish between true and false spiritual influences — to recognize the work of God's Spirit, the natural human spirit, and the deceiving spirits of demons; listed among the gifts of the Spirit in 1 Corinthians 12 and required of the whole church in 1 John 4.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 12:10
To another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discerning of spirits; to another divers kinds of tongues.
1 John 4:1
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
1 Thessalonians 5:21
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
corruption_summary: Either dismissed as charismatic-only or wielded irresponsibly; both fail the church.
corruption_paragraphs: Some Christians dismiss the gift as cessationist policy; others claim it as license to declare everyone they dislike demonic. Scripture grants it as a Spirit-given ability tested by doctrinal soundness (1 John 4:2-3) and by fruit (Matt 7:16). Use it carefully.
usage: Test the spirits; do not believe every one.

etymology: Greek dokimazō — to test, prove, examine.
biblical_def: The self-examination Paul commands before the Lord's Supper (1 Cor 11:28) and as ongoing discipleship: 'Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith' (2 Cor 13:5).
webster_summary: Spiritual self-examination, especially before communion.
webster_full: The disciplined self-testing Paul commands — examining oneself before participating in the Lord's Supper, and more broadly examining whether one is in the faith. The Greek dokimazō is a coin-testing metaphor: putting yourself to genuine test.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 11:28
But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.
2 Corinthians 13:5
Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves.
Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts.
corruption_summary: Replaced with 'don't be too hard on yourself'; Paul commands the harder discipline.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern devotion runs from self-examination as legalism. Paul commands it. The unexamined life eats and drinks unworthily; the examined life finds the cross afresh. Distinguish self-examination (Spirit-led, gospel-grounded) from morbid introspection (self-flagellation). Both are real categories.

etymology: Greek sōphrosynē — soundness of mind, soberness.
biblical_def: Sound-mindedness; clear-headed seriousness; the disposition Paul commands in Titus 2:12 ('live soberly') and Peter in 1 Peter 5:8 ('be sober, be vigilant').
webster_summary: Sound-minded clear-headed seriousness.
webster_full: Sound-mindedness, clear-headed seriousness, free from intoxication of mind by drink, passion, error, or fantasy; the disposition required of believers, of women in Titus 2, of leaders, and of all in Peter's eschatological warning.
scriptures: Titus 2:12
Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world.
1 Peter 5:8
Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour.
1 Peter 1:13
Wherefore gird up the loins of your mind, be sober, and hope to the end.
corruption_summary: Reduced to not-being-drunk; Greek sōphrosynē is the wider sound-mindedness.
corruption_paragraphs: Sōphrosynē is one of the four cardinal virtues. It includes sobriety from drink but extends much further: sobriety of mind, of imagination, of speculation, of emotion. Cultivate sound-mindedness as a core Christian virtue.
usage: Live soberly in this present world.

etymology: From Italian all'erta "on the watchtower."
biblical_def: Watchful attention; commanded by Christ ('watch and pray') and Paul ('watch ye, stand fast in the faith'); especially required in last-days awareness (Mark 13:33; 1 Cor 16:13).
webster_summary: Watchful attention; commanded by Christ.
webster_full: Watchful attention to spiritual realities and dangers; the disposition Christ commands ('watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation'), Paul renews ('watch ye, stand fast in the faith'), and Peter applies eschatologically ('the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer').
scriptures: Mark 13:33
Take ye heed, watch and pray: for ye know not when the time is.
1 Corinthians 16:13
Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
1 Peter 4:7
But the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer.
corruption_summary: Replaced by general anxiety; Christian alertness is specifically directed toward Christ's coming, devil's schemes, and brotherly need.
corruption_paragraphs: Christian alertness is not free-floating anxiety; it is targeted attention. Watch for the Lord's coming. Watch for the devil's schemes. Watch for brothers in trouble. Watch your own heart. Anxiety scatters; alertness focuses.
roots_summary: Greek grēgoreō — to watch, be alert.

etymology: Originally "wicked"; later "sharp-witted, prudent."
biblical_def: Sharp-witted, prudent in dealing; commanded by Christ in the parable of the unjust steward (Luke 16:8) and the dove-and-serpent saying (Matt 10:16).
webster_summary: Sharp-witted prudence in dealing.
webster_full: Sharp-witted prudence in practical affairs; in Luke 16 Jesus calls the unjust steward 'wise' (phronimōs) — meaning shrewd — and notes that the children of light should be at least as shrewd as the children of this world; in Matthew 10 the disciples are sent forth wise as serpents.
scriptures: Luke 16:8
And the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely (shrewdly): for the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light.
Matthew 10:16
Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
Proverbs 22:3
A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.
corruption_summary: Confused with cunning or manipulation; biblical shrewdness is prudent foresight in good causes.
corruption_paragraphs: Shrewd in modern English often connotes manipulation. Biblical shrewdness is prudent practical wisdom — Joseph in Egypt, Daniel in Babylon, Paul before Felix. Christians should be shrewd for kingdom purposes, not naive in a wolf-world.
usage: Be shrewd as serpents, harmless as doves.

etymology: From Christ's saying in Matthew 10:16.
biblical_def: The shrewd practical wisdom Christ commands of His disciples in mission — being aware of dangers, careful in speech, prudent in action — paired always with dove-harmlessness.
webster_summary: Shrewd missional prudence paired with harmlessness.
webster_full: The shrewd practical wisdom Christ commands of His disciples in mission — aware of dangers, careful in speech, prudent in action; deliberately paired with dove-harmlessness so that prudence does not slide into deceit.
scriptures: Matthew 10:16
Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
Genesis 3:1
Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made.
Proverbs 14:15
The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going.
corruption_summary: Cited by half — 'wise as serpents' without 'harmless as doves' — yielding scheming Christianity.
corruption_paragraphs: The pairing matters. Serpent-wise without dove-harmless becomes manipulation; dove-harmless without serpent-wise becomes naive. Christ's missional ethic requires both: shrewd in awareness, innocent in motive. Hold them together.
usage: Wise as serpents AND harmless as doves.

etymology: From Christ's saying in Matthew 10:16; Greek akeraioi — unmixed, pure.
biblical_def: The pure-motivated innocence Christ pairs with serpent-wisdom — shrewd in awareness without scheming, prudent without manipulation, alert without paranoid (Matt 10:16; Phil 2:15).
webster_summary: Pure-motivated innocence paired with shrewd wisdom.
webster_full: The pure-motivated innocence Christ requires of His disciples — Greek akeraioi means 'unmixed' — paired with serpent-wisdom in His missional ethic; the same word Paul uses for the Philippians who are to be 'blameless and harmless' children of God in a crooked generation.
scriptures: Matthew 10:16
Be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
Philippians 2:15
That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation.
Romans 16:19
I would have you wise unto that which is good, and simple concerning evil.
corruption_summary: Equated with naivety or doormat-ism; biblical harmlessness is pure motive matched with prudent action.
corruption_paragraphs: Harmlessness is not weakness; it is purity of motive. Christ Himself was harmless — and He turned over tables when needed. Harmlessness means no scheming, no malice, no manipulation. It does not mean no action, no truth, no boundaries.
usage: Harmless as doves AND wise as serpents.
Pure motive matched with prudent action.

etymology: From Greek Mentor, the guide of Telemachus in the Odyssey; modern term for the discipling relationship.
biblical_def: The personal life-on-life shaping of one disciple by an older — modeled by Moses-Joshua, Elijah-Elisha, Paul-Timothy; not a program but a relationship of imitation and instruction (2 Tim 2:2; 1 Cor 11:1).
webster_summary: Personal life-on-life discipling relationship.
webster_full: The personal, life-on-life shaping of one disciple by an older through teaching, modeling, and faithful presence; modeled in Scripture by Moses-Joshua, Elijah-Elisha, Naomi-Ruth, Paul-Timothy and Paul-Titus; commanded as 2 Timothy 2:2 — entrust to faithful men who will teach others also.
scriptures: 2 Timothy 2:2
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
1 Corinthians 11:1
Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ.
Titus 2:3-4
The aged women likewise... that they may teach the young women to be sober.
corruption_summary: Replaced by programmatic discipleship classes; the personal life-on-life element is what Paul actually modeled.
corruption_paragraphs: Programs cannot substitute for mentoring. Paul did not run Timothy through a class; he traveled with him, prayed with him, suffered with him, and wrote to him. Mentoring takes time and presence. Reclaim it as central, not supplemental.
usage: Entrust to faithful men who teach others.

etymology: Composite term for the New Testament pattern of multiplying disciples.
biblical_def: The pattern Paul describes in 2 Timothy 2:2: paul → timothy → faithful men → others — four spiritual generations in one verse, the multiplication framework of all biblical discipleship.
webster_summary: Four-generation discipleship multiplication pattern.
webster_full: The pattern Paul names in 2 Timothy 2:2 — what you heard of me, commit to faithful men, who shall teach others also — four spiritual generations in one verse: Paul → Timothy → faithful men → others. The framework for all biblical discipleship multiplication.
scriptures: 2 Timothy 2:2
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Matthew 28:19-20
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations... Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you.
1 Thessalonians 1:6-8
And ye became followers of us, and of the Lord... so that ye were ensamples to all that believe.
corruption_summary: Replaced by attractional crowds; the patient four-generation pattern requires deliberate, costly investment.
corruption_paragraphs: Multiplication beats addition. Paul invests in a few; they invest in a few; soon a movement. Modern church culture often runs on attractional addition, which produces crowds but few disciples. Reclaim the four-generation pattern.
usage: Entrust to faithful men who entrust to others.

etymology: Reference to Titus 2:3-5 — the older women's mentoring role.
biblical_def: Paul's commissioning of older women in Titus 2:3-5 to teach the younger to love their husbands, love their children, be sober, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient — woman-to-woman discipleship.
webster_summary: Older women mentoring younger women per Titus 2.
webster_full: Paul's commissioning in Titus 2:3-5 of older women to be teachers of good things — instructing younger women in marriage, motherhood, household management, character, and reverent life; a specifically feminine line of discipleship paralleling the Paul-Timothy line.
scriptures: Titus 2:3-5

The aged women likewise, that they be in behaviour as becometh holiness, not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things; That they may teach the young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children, To be discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient to their own husbands.
1 Timothy 5:9-10
Let not a widow be taken into the number under threescore years old... well reported of for good works.
Proverbs 31:26
She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness.
corruption_summary: Sidelined as outdated gender roles; Paul commands it as essential to healthy churches.
corruption_paragraphs: Titus 2 women are a structural necessity. Without older women teaching younger women, the church loses a whole line of formation. The pattern requires older women whose lives qualify them to teach. Pray for Titus 2 women in your congregation.
usage: Older women teach younger; the pattern is structural.

etymology: Greek presbytidas — older / elder women.
biblical_def: The category Paul honors and commissions in Titus 2:3 — women whose age, godliness, and experience qualify them to teach; honored as 'mothers' (1 Tim 5:2) in the household of faith.
webster_summary: Honored and commissioned in Titus 2 to teach.
webster_full: The honored category of older women in the New Testament — to be addressed as 'mothers' (1 Tim 5:2), to live in a manner becoming holiness (Titus 2:3), to be teachers of good things to younger women, and to provide the wisdom-bench of the local church.
scriptures: Titus 2:3
The aged women likewise, that they be in behaviour as becometh holiness... teachers of good things.
1 Timothy 5:2
The elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, with all purity.
Proverbs 31:28
Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her.
corruption_summary: Devalued by youth-cult; Scripture honors them as mothers and teachers.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern culture's youth-cult sidelines older women. Scripture seats them at the wisdom-bench. Honor them as mothers; learn from them; commission them to teach. The church without older women is missing a chamber.

etymology: Greek neas — younger.
biblical_def: The category Paul commits to the older women's care in Titus 2:4-5; to be taught by example to love husbands, love children, be sober, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient.
webster_summary: To be discipled by older women per Titus 2.
webster_full: The category of younger women in the New Testament — to be addressed as 'sisters with all purity' (1 Tim 5:2), to be discipled by older women in Titus 2 essentials of household, marriage, motherhood, character, and worship.
scriptures: Titus 2:4-5
That they may teach the young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children, To be discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient to their own husbands.
1 Timothy 5:14
I will therefore that the younger women marry, bear children, guide the house, give none occasion to the adversary.
1 Timothy 5:2
The younger as sisters, with all purity.
corruption_summary: Often left undiscipled in modern church structures; Paul commands the relationship as essential.
corruption_paragraphs: Younger women need Titus 2 mentors. Without them, marriage, motherhood, and household management get learned by Instagram. Pray for the older women in your church to step into the role; pray for younger women to seek it.

etymology: Composite from biblical shepherd imagery — Hebrew roeh, Greek poimēn.
biblical_def: Christ's pattern of leadership: feeding the flock, knowing the sheep by name, going before them, laying down life for them; the pattern for elders (1 Pet 5:1-4) and contrasted with hireling-style leadership (John 10:11-14).
webster_summary: Christ's flock-feeding life-laying pattern of leadership.
webster_full: The pattern of leadership Christ embodies as the Good Shepherd — feeding the flock, knowing each sheep by name, going before them, laying down life for them — and which He commits to elders to imitate; contrasted with hireling-style leadership that flees when wolves come.
scriptures: John 10:11
I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
1 Peter 5:2-3
Feed the flock of God which is among you... not for filthy lucre... neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
Ezekiel 34:2
Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?
corruption_summary: Replaced by CEO-style or celebrity-style leadership; Scripture insists on the shepherd model.
corruption_paragraphs: The CEO model treats people as resources; the celebrity model treats them as audience; the shepherd model treats them as sheep — known, fed, defended, sacrificed-for. Ezekiel 34 indicts the shepherd-leaders who fed themselves; Christ in John 10 is the answer.

etymology: Compound under + shepherd; the office of a pastor under the Chief Shepherd.
biblical_def: The pastor or elder serving under Christ the Chief Shepherd; accountable to Him for the flock entrusted (1 Pet 5:2-4; Heb 13:17, 20).
webster_summary: Pastor serving under Christ the Chief Shepherd.
webster_full: The pastor or elder considered as a shepherd under Christ the Chief Shepherd; entrusted with care of a portion of the flock and accountable to the Chief Shepherd at His appearing for that stewardship.
scriptures: 1 Peter 5:2-4
Feed the flock of God which is among you... And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away.
Hebrews 13:17
Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account.
Hebrews 13:20
Now the God of peace, that brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great shepherd of the sheep.
corruption_summary: Inflated to high-status position; Scripture frames it as humble service under Christ's authority.
corruption_paragraphs: Pastors are undershepherds — under Christ. The flock is His; pastors are stewards. The Chief Shepherd is coming, and pastors will give account. This frame humbles the office and dignifies the labor.

etymology: Greek poimnion tou theou — flock of God.
biblical_def: Peter's term for the local church under elder care (1 Pet 5:2) — a flock that is God's, entrusted to elders who must feed, not fleece, them.
webster_summary: The local church as God's flock entrusted to elders.
webster_full: Peter's term for the local church considered as a flock — God's flock, not the elders'; entrusted by Christ for the elders to feed, oversee, and lead by example, with Christ the Chief Shepherd evaluating their care at His coming.
scriptures: 1 Peter 5:2
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind.
Acts 20:28
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
John 10:16
And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring.
corruption_summary: Treated as 'my church' by leaders; Peter insists it is God's flock, not theirs.
corruption_paragraphs: The flock belongs to God. Pastors do not own the church; they steward it. Acts 20:28 settles it: He purchased it with His own blood. The elder who treats the flock as his own commodity has misunderstood his office.
usage: The flock is God's, not the pastor's.
Feed it; do not fleece it.

etymology: Hebrew shevet and mish'enet — shepherd's tools.
biblical_def: The shepherd's two tools in Psalm 23:4 — the rod (shevet) for protection from predators and discipline of straying sheep, the staff (mish'enet) for support and gentle direction; together they comfort.
webster_summary: The shepherd's two tools: rod for defense, staff for guidance.
webster_full: The shepherd's twin instruments named in Psalm 23:4 — the rod (a heavy club) for defense against predators and discipline of straying sheep, and the staff (a longer crook) for support, rescue, and gentle direction. Together they comfort the flock.
scriptures: Psalm 23:4
Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.
Micah 7:14
Feed thy people with thy rod, the flock of thine heritage.
Hebrews 12:6
For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.
corruption_summary: Romanticized as gentle imagery, missing how the rod also disciplines and how both together comfort.
corruption_paragraphs: Both tools comfort. The rod that drives off wolves also disciplines straying sheep. The staff that supports also pulls back. Pastoral care that uses staff without rod becomes permissive; rod without staff becomes harsh. The Good Shepherd uses both.
usage: Pastoral care uses rod and staff.

etymology: Greek poimainō — to shepherd, feed.
biblical_def: Christ's command to Peter (John 21:15-17) and to all elders (Acts 20:28; 1 Pet 5:2) — provide spiritual food (the Word) to the flock as the primary task of pastoral office.
webster_summary: The primary pastoral task of Word-feeding.
webster_full: The primary pastoral task: provide spiritual food (the preached and taught Word) to the flock; commanded by Christ to Peter ('feed my sheep'), to the Ephesian elders ('feed the church of God'), and to all elders by Peter ('feed the flock of God').
scriptures: John 21:17
He saith unto him the third time, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me? ... Feed my sheep.
Acts 20:28
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock... to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
1 Peter 5:2
Feed the flock of God which is among you.
corruption_summary: Replaced by entertainment, programs, or platform; the irreducible pastoral task is Word-feeding.
corruption_paragraphs: Sheep need food. Christians need the Word. The pastor's irreducible task is to feed them — through preaching, teaching, and personal care that brings Scripture to life. Anything that displaces Word-feeding misses the office. Peter heard 'feed my sheep' three times for a reason.
usage: Feed the flock; that is the office.
Three times Christ said it; once is not enough.

etymology: From 1 Timothy 3:1-7 and Titus 1:5-9.
biblical_def: The biblical list of character and competence requirements for the office of elder — above reproach, husband of one wife, sober, hospitable, apt to teach, gentle, not greedy, manages own household well (1 Tim 3:1-7; Titus 1:5-9).
webster_summary: Paul's character/competence list in 1 Tim 3 / Titus 1.
webster_full: The Pauline list in 1 Timothy 3:1-7 and Titus 1:5-9 of character and competence requirements for elder office: above reproach, husband of one wife, sober, hospitable, apt to teach, not given to wine, gentle, not contentious, not greedy, manages own household well, not a novice, well-reported by outsiders.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 3:1-3

If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work. A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach; Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre.
Titus 1:6-9
If any be blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children... For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry.
1 Peter 5:1-4
The elders which are among you I exhort... Feed the flock of God.
corruption_summary: Watered down or replaced by skill-based criteria; Paul's list is overwhelmingly character.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's qualifications list is overwhelmingly character with one competence (apt to teach). Modern church search committees often invert this: emphasizing competencies and minimizing character. The result is the parade of fallen leaders. Restore the order: character first.
usage: Apt to teach is one of many; the rest is character.

etymology: From 1 Timothy 3:8-13.
biblical_def: The biblical list for the office of deacon — grave, not double-tongued, not given to much wine, not greedy, holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience, tested first, husband of one wife, ruling children well (1 Tim 3:8-13).
webster_summary: Paul's deacon-character list in 1 Tim 3.
webster_full: The list in 1 Timothy 3:8-13 of character requirements for deacons — grave, not double-tongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre, holding the faith with pure conscience, first proved (tested), blameless, husbands of one wife, ruling children and households well.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 3:8-10

Likewise must the deacons be grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre; Holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience. And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless.
1 Timothy 3:12
Let the deacons be the husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own houses well.
Acts 6:3
Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom.
corruption_summary: Treated as a lesser office requiring lesser standards; Paul's list is nearly as rigorous as the elder's.
corruption_paragraphs: Deacon is not a junior or training role; it is its own honorable office with its own qualifications. Paul's deacon list is nearly as rigorous as his elder list. Honor the office; vet candidates carefully; let them first be proved.
usage: Honor the deacon office; vet carefully.

etymology: Greek pistos ho logos — "trustworthy is the saying."
biblical_def: Five sayings in the Pastoral Epistles introduced by 'this is a faithful saying,' likely circulating apostolic-era confessional formulas (1 Tim 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Tim 2:11; Titus 3:8).
webster_summary: Apostolic-era confessional formulas in the Pastorals.
webster_full: Five sayings in the Pastoral Epistles introduced by 'this is a faithful saying' (Greek pistos ho logos) — likely circulating apostolic-era confessional formulas Paul commends as trustworthy: that Christ Jesus came to save sinners (1 Tim 1:15); that to desire the bishop's office is to desire a good work (3:1); that godliness is profitable (4:9); that if we died with Him we shall live with Him (2 Tim 2:11); that good works should be maintained (Titus 3:8).
scriptures: 1 Timothy 1:15
This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.
1 Timothy 4:9-10
This is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptation. For therefore we both labour and suffer reproach, because we trust in the living God.
2 Timothy 2:11
It is a faithful saying: For if we be dead with him, we shall also live with him.
corruption_summary: Read past as filler; missing the recognition that Paul is citing five distinct apostolic-era confessions.
corruption_paragraphs: When Paul says 'this is a faithful saying,' he is not warming up — he is citing. Five times in the Pastorals. Each citation is a snapshot of early Christian confession. Read them as the apostolic doctrinal core.
usage: Five faithful sayings; learn all five.

etymology: Greek mias gynaikos andra — literally "a one-woman man."
biblical_def: Paul's first qualification for elder and deacon (1 Tim 3:2, 12; Titus 1:6) — not 'married only once' but 'a one-woman man' — devoted in heart, eyes, and conduct to his wife alone.
webster_summary: Paul's qualification: a one-woman man.
webster_full: Paul's qualification for elder and deacon, literally 'a man of one woman' — emphasizing not marital math (married once vs. remarried) but heart-devotion to one woman; the marker of a man whose eyes, affections, and conduct belong to his wife alone.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 3:2
A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach.
1 Timothy 3:12
Let the deacons be the husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own houses well.
Titus 1:6
If any be blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children not accused of riot or unruly.
corruption_summary: Reduced to 'never been divorced'; the deeper requirement is heart-faithfulness regardless of past.
corruption_paragraphs: A widower who remarried is still a one-woman man. A man married once but with a wandering eye is not. Paul's phrase is heart-language. Do not weaponize it against grace; do not weaken it against character. A one-woman man — known by his wife and his church.
usage: A one-woman man — heart, eyes, conduct.
Do not weaponize the phrase; do not weaken it.

etymology: Composite from biblical household-management requirements for elders.
biblical_def: The household ordered under God's lordship; required of elders ('one that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity') as the test before church-leadership (1 Tim 3:4-5; Titus 1:6).
webster_summary: Household ordered under God; required of elders.
webster_full: The household ordered under God's lordship — husband and wife in covenant love, children in respectful subjection, household worship and instruction central; required by Paul as test of elder readiness ('if a man know not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God?').
scriptures: 1 Timothy 3:4-5
One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity; (For if a man know not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God?)
Joshua 24:15
But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
Acts 16:31
Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house.
corruption_summary: Privatized to 'whatever works for your family'; Scripture treats it as a test of public office and a sphere of God's covenant blessing.
corruption_paragraphs: Joshua's choice — me and my house — is corporate. Paul's elder qualification — manages his own household well — is public. The household is not a private compartment; it is the proving-ground of leadership. Build godly households first.
usage: Build the household before the office.
Me and my house, we will serve the Lord.

etymology: Greek chēra ontōs — really a widow; Paul's category in 1 Timothy 5.
biblical_def: Paul's category in 1 Timothy 5:3-16 for the widow without family support, of advanced age, faithful character, who depends on the church's care; distinguished from younger widows who should remarry.
webster_summary: Widow alone, aged, faithful — under church care.
webster_full: Paul's category in 1 Timothy 5:3-16 for the widow who is 'really a widow' — without family support, advanced in years (60+), of faithful character, given to good works — and therefore eligible for ongoing church care; distinguished from younger widows who are urged to remarry.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 5:3
Honour widows that are widows indeed.
1 Timothy 5:9-10
Let not a widow be taken into the number under threescore years old, having been the wife of one man, Well reported of for good works.
1 Timothy 5:14
I will therefore that the younger women marry, bear children, guide the house.
corruption_summary: Either ignored entirely (no widow-care system in modern churches) or applied indiscriminately, missing Paul's careful distinctions.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's widow-care system is detailed: family first, then church, with criteria. Modern churches often have neither system nor criteria. Recover the care-of-widows ministry — pure religion before the Father visits widows in their affliction (James 1:27).
usage: Family first, then church, with criteria.
